newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Doctors say Yeltsin to have surgery, date unknown.
newsitem.headline: Doctors say Yeltsin to have surgery, date unknown.

text.p: Cardiologists decided on Wednesday that Russian President Boris Yeltsin should undergo heart surgery but set no date for an operation crucial for stability and fragile reforms in the world's biggest country.
To minimise risks, it will take six to eight weeks to prepare him for surgery to improve the blood supply to the heart, the team of doctors said.

The delay opens up a prospect of more political uncertainty about Yeltsin's grip on power. Mikhail Gorbachev, last president of the Soviet Union, promptly urged him to resign, saying illness had prevented him from working for many months.
But an American adviser said the operation would soon restore the ailing leader to "normal".
Russian surgeon Andrei Vorobyov, heading the council of doctors, said Yeltsin's heavy workload during a summer of electioneering had "caused complications which make the operation undesirable today."
The go-ahead came after Russian and foreign specialists examined the 65-year-old Kremlin leader at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital.
"The doctors' council took a decision to carry out an operation on President Boris Yeltsin's heart," Interfax news agency said.
The group, responsible for a medical procedure with huge political ramifications, saw Yeltsin during a meeting which lasted about three hours.
The doctors' council, which included pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, was earlier expected to set a date and conditions for heart bypass surgery.
DeBakey told a newsbriefing: "After reviewing all facts I am pleased to say that the operation is needed, that it shall provide excellent results.
"After the operation the president will soon be restored to normal."

The undercurrent of instability in Russia was underlined on Wednesday by security chief Alexander Lebed, who told a Moscow newspaper that the government's failure to pay soldiers' wages could soon spark military uprisings. "An armed mutiny may take place this autumn," Lebed told the Vechernyaya Moskva daily.
Yeltsin has been in hospital since September 13 and aides say doctors are conducting tests and preparing him for a bypass operation.

His prolonged absence from the Kremlin has fuelled speculation about political intrigues and a possible struggle for influence between Lebed, who makes no secret of his presidential ambitions, and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Kremlin officials have condemned the rumour-mongering as indecent and say the president is in full control of affairs of state, working on documents for up to 2-1/2 hours a day.
Yeltsin himself has said surgery is needed if he is to lead an active political life. The operation, which usually involves bypassing damaged arteries with ones from the leg, is common.
The risk of dying is about five percent in Russia, but doctors say it could be greater for Yeltsin if he has serious liver or kidney problems which have not been disclosed.
Russian officials have said DeBakey, 88, is advising the Russian team but will not take part in the operation itself.
Chief surgeon Renat Akchurin on Tuesday ruled out cancelling the surgery -- a statement that bolstered Russian shares on Wednesday, lifting prices by about one percent in early trade.

Akchurin, who is expected to lead the team that will operate on the president, said in a television interview at the weekend that the surgery could be postponed for up to two months to allow Yeltsin to prepare better and gain strength.
Interfax news agency said Akchurin would head to the German city of Hanover to consult with specialists there after the doctors' meeting with Yeltsin.
The liberal newspaper Sevodnya said cancellation or a lengthy postponement of the operation could plunge Russia into uncertainty that Yeltsin's opponents were sure to exploit.
"Even if an operation is not necessary on patient Yeltsin, President Yeltsin will have to be operated on," Sevodnya said. "Otherwise, he can expect to face a major scandal."
Russia's communist opposition have already accused Yeltsin of deceiving the electorate in the July 3 poll, which gave him another four years in office, and suggested he should resign.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and Akchurin said he may have had a third between the first and second rounds of voting. At the time, Yeltsin disappeared from public view but aides insisted that he was merely exhausted and had a cold.
Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's stand-in under the constitution, said on Tuesday Yeltsin's resignation now was out of the question.
Yeltsin has already handed over some powers to Chernomyrdin and said he would put the prime minister in complete charge while he is being operated on.
